questions.question: Why can a diabetes-related plantar ulcer be painless yet high risk?
choices: Loss of protective sensation can mask repetitive pressure injury and infection
Pain is always required for ulcer severity
Diabetes prevents skin breakdown
Plantar ulcers never involve bone
questions.explanation: Neuropathy can remove the pain signal that would normally prompt protection. Painless ulcers can still be deep, infected, ischemic, or at risk for amputation.

questions.question: Which components belong in a comprehensive diabetes foot examination?
choices: Skin and nail inspection, deformity assessment, neurologic sensation testing, pulses or vascular assessment, and footwear review
Only a blood glucose measurement
Only a photograph of the toes
Only asking whether pain is present
questions.explanation: Limb-risk assessment requires skin, deformity, sensation, vascular status, footwear, history, and symptoms. A painless foot can still have major risk.

questions.question: What does a chronic wound culture alone establish?
choices: It proves the wound is clinically infected
It may show colonization and must be interpreted with clinical signs of infection
It determines ulcer depth
It excludes osteomyelitis
questions.explanation: Chronic wounds are commonly colonized. Infection is diagnosed clinically using local and systemic inflammatory signs, wound progression, and patient context, not a culture result alone.

questions.question: Which combination is most concerning for urgent limb-threatening disease?
choices: Fever, spreading erythema, foul drainage, gangrene or ischemic color change, and weak pulses
Stable dry skin with intact sensation
An old healed blister
Mild callus without skin break
questions.explanation: Systemic illness, progressive infection, necrosis or gangrene, and perfusion concerns can threaten limb and life. These patients need emergency or expedited multidisciplinary evaluation.

questions.question: Why is offloading considered treatment for a neuropathic plantar ulcer?
choices: It reduces repetitive pressure that prevents healing
It replaces wound assessment and vascular evaluation
It makes infection impossible
It is only cosmetic
questions.explanation: Pressure is part of the pathophysiology of many neuropathic ulcers. Offloading addresses that mechanism but must be selected in the context of infection, ischemia, balance, and specialist direction.

questions.question: A neuropathic patient has a warm swollen red foot after minor trauma with little pain and no clear skin break. What condition should be considered?
choices: Acute Charcot neuroarthropathy
Only uncomplicated cellulitis
Simple dry skin
Diabetic retinopathy
questions.explanation: A hot swollen relatively painless foot in a patient with neuropathy can represent Charcot neuroarthropathy. Continued weight bearing can cause structural collapse, so urgent offloading and specialty assessment are important.

questions.question: Which approach is appropriate when osteomyelitis is suspected in a diabetes-related foot ulcer?
choices: Use focused examination and initial studies such as probe-to-bone, plain radiographs, and inflammatory markers when clinically indicated, with specialist input as needed
Rely only on a superficial swab
Assume normal pain excludes bone involvement
Delay all assessment until the ulcer closes
questions.explanation: Osteomyelitis assessment integrates clinical findings with targeted tests. Further imaging and specialty consultation may be needed depending on the likelihood and initial results.

questions.question: Why must peripheral artery disease be assessed in a diabetic foot ulcer?
choices: Perfusion affects healing, infection response, debridement, and need for vascular intervention
Pulses are irrelevant to ulcers
PAD only affects the upper extremity
Antibiotics correct ischemia
questions.explanation: Inadequate arterial perfusion can prevent healing and worsen infection. Antibiotics and dressing changes cannot substitute for vascular assessment or revascularization when indicated.

questions.question: Which patient generally needs more frequent foot inspection and specialty surveillance?
choices: A patient with sensory loss and prior ulceration
A patient with no diabetes and no foot symptoms
A patient with a single normal foot examination only
A patient who prefers sandals
questions.explanation: Sensory loss, PAD, deformity, prior ulcer or amputation, kidney failure, and other high-risk features increase ulcer risk and warrant more frequent evaluation.

questions.question: What is the central principle of diabetic foot limb preservation?
choices: Address wound, infection, pressure, perfusion, glycemic and vascular risk, patient capacity, and referral together
Treat every wound with antibiotics only
Wait for pain before examining the feet
Focus on glucose alone
questions.explanation: The diabetic foot is a systems problem. Successful limb preservation combines wound care, offloading, infection assessment, vascular evaluation, risk-factor control, and practical follow-up.
